newsitem.title: USA: White House, Republicans talk on taxes, spending.
newsitem.headline: White House, Republicans talk on taxes, spending.

text.p: Republicans and White House officials began outlining areas of possible compromise on Thursday in trying to bridge differences on a tax cut package.

Capitol Hill was rife with meetings between Republicans, Democrats and administration officials, with negotiators shuttling between Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott's office, House Speaker Newt Gingrich's office and other locales.

House and Senate leaders are trying to strike a compromise with the White House on tax and spending bills that would enact a May agreement to balance the budget over five years and provide $85 billion net tax cuts.

"I think we're making some progress, we're getting serious ... and trying to see if we can't get this deal tied up in a couple of days," Assistant Senate Majority Leader Don Nickles said. "We started letting them know where we're willing to compromise and vice versa," the Oklahoma Republican added.
The administration also said progress was being made. "We had a very useful discussion around the areas we need to deal with," Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said.
House and Senate Republicans earlier this week arrived at a unified tax plan that received a cool reception from the White House.

One area still undecided is whether to include a Senate proposal for a 20-cents-per-pack increase in the federal cigarette tax to raise about $15 billion over five years, $8 billion of which would go to fund children's health programmes. President Clinton has endorsed that approach.
"I don't think it's at all certain we're going to keep the cigarette tax, that has not at all been decided," House Ways and Means Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, said.

Some Republicans who were not part of the main tax talks said they had heard of a Republican proposal to include the cigarette tax, but not earmark the funds for children's health and were angered by that.

White House Budget Director Franklin Raines said the two sides were split on the children's health plan. The White House wants $24 billion, including $8 billion from the cigarette tax increase. But House Republicans have said there was not much support on their side to raise the cigarette tax.
Gingrich sounded hopeful that compromise would be reached in the major tax areas.

"We had a very good meeting," the Georgia Republican said. "We really do hope to have the educational tax credit ... the $500 per child credit. We also think we will be able to work out the estate tax rates for small businesses and family farms and a cut in the capital gains."

Republicans have rejigged the structure of a $500 per-child tax credit so that it could be kept in a special account for up to three years for low-income families who do not owe income tax after receiving other tax breaks.

Those families would be allowed to receive the child credit once they owed some income tax. The structure of the child credit is a key sticking point with the White House which wants the credit to go to low-income families, including as a government payment if they owe no income taxes.
After the last tax meeting broke for the evening, tax negotiators said none of the major issues had been resolved.

"We just ping-ponged around again on six or seven issues, largely restatements of what's been said before," John Hilley, White House legislative director, said. "I think it was a good day overall in terms of understanding."
Tax and spending talks were to resume Friday as Republicans aim to finish the legislation by Aug. 1.
The White House and Republicans said they were narrowing their differences, but did not make any major decisions on Medicare, Medicaid and welfare issues.

Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, continued to press the White House to accept Senate-passed plans to gradually raise the Medicare eligibility age to 67 from 65, institute a $5 co-payment for home health services and make well-off beneficiaries pay more for doctor's care.

The White House is refusing to budge on the first two issues. While Clinton is willing to support an income-test he wants it administered with the Internal Revenue Service, which Republicans fear will be seen as a tax increase.
